STA3115 EXPLORATORY DATA ANALYSIS, FINAL PROJECT

Exploring Bicycle Imbalances

Group 1, November 26, 2026

Hello everyone. We’re Group 1, and today we’ll talk about Ddareungi, Seoul’s public bike service. Many of you have probably used it around campus or elsewhere in Seoul. We explored how bicycles move between stations and the imbalances that arise.

Photos: *Youngjin, CC BY-SA 3.0 (left); Sarang, public domain (right); Wikimedia Commons. Facts: Seoul Metropolitan Government, 2024 and 2025.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

First, a quick introduction for anyone who has not used Ddareungi. You rent a bike through the app by scanning its QR code. Then you ride to your destination and return it by locking it at any station. You do not have to return it to the station where you started. This means bicycles move between stations as people travel around the city.

WHY THIS MATTERS

A growing operating deficit

Operating deficit · 2022 → 2025

₩9.4 bn → ₩17.6 bn

Nearly doubled in three years

Redistribution staff time

53%

of operating cost, according to Bike Magazine

Redistribution moves bicycles from stations with a surplus to those with shortages.

Understanding these imbalances can help the city assess redistribution needs.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

We began with the operating deficit. It grew from 9.4 billion won in 2022 to 17.6 billion won in 2025, nearly doubling in three years. This led us to look at the costs of running the service. According to Bike Magazine, 53% of operating cost is staff time spent redistributing bicycles. This is the work of moving bikes from stations with a surplus to stations with shortages. That made redistribution an important motivation for our study. We wanted to provide insights by understanding the factors associated with bicycle imbalances and shortages.

Our Question

What station characteristics are associated with persistent bicycle imbalances,
and why do some stations experience shortages?

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

With this in mind, we wanted to understand what station characteristics are associated with persistent bicycle imbalances and why some stations experience shortages. We looked at both where bicycles tend to leave and where none are available. We hope these patterns can provide useful reference information when the city assesses redistribution needs.

DATA

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

To answer it, we use every trip between Seoul's bike stations in 2024 and 2025. Of the 731 days, 720 have clean records: we dropped ten days where rentals and returns did not match, and one empty file. Then we keep weekdays that are not public holidays, 482 days, and of those the dry ones, under 1 mm of rain: 378 days. Weekends follow a different pattern from the commute, and rain changes how many people ride. That leaves 2,843 stations with records on at least 50 of those days. We also use the hourly bikes at every station in 2025, weather from 27 weather stations, elevation from the city's contour map, and the subway stations. Next: what we measure on those days.

WHAT WE MEASURE

Losing bikes vs running out

Net outflow: rentals minus returns, in bikes. Above 0, the station loses bikes; below 0, it gains them.
Empty share: how often the station has zero bikes at 7, 8 or 9 am.

63%

of stations lose bikes every morning: net outflow above 0 (1,697 of 2,713)

24%

of those have empty share ≥20%: empty in at least one in five morning readings (402)

Net outflow: 7 to 9 am, dry weekdays 2024 to 2025 (team table). Empty share: hourly stock, dry weekdays 2025.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

We use two measures. The first is net outflow: rentals minus returns, counted in bikes. When it is positive, the station loses bikes; when it is negative, it gains them. We compute it for the whole day and for the morning commute; a daily net outflow of plus 4 means the station loses four bikes a day on average through user trips. Net outflow tells us where bikes leave. But our question is where they run out, so the second measure is the empty share: how often the station has no bike at all at 7, 8 or 9 am. Each dot is one station. Everything right of the line loses bikes in the morning: 63% of all stations. But only the red ones, above the dashed line, are empty in at least one in five readings, and that is just 24% of the stations that lose bikes. The blue stations have empty share below 20%; they can still run out, just less frequently. We keep both measures from here on. We considered time of day, weather, terrain and distance to the subway. First, we look at the usage patterns that help explain our choice of days and commute hours.

FACTOR 1. TIME OF DAY

Rides by hour

8 am, 6 pm

two sharp weekday peaks, with 11,300 and 13,200 rides in the hour

on weekends and holidays, highest at 5 pm with 6,900 rides

Weekdays only

from here on, with the 7–9 am commute as the key window

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

We first considered time of day and weather. On weekdays, usage peaks at 8 am and 6 pm, following the commuting hours. Weekends and holidays have a broad afternoon peak instead. Weather also affects how much people ride. We therefore focused on non-holiday weekdays with less than 1 mm of rainfall, especially the 7–9 am commute. The detailed temperature findings are available in the appendix. Within this scope, we next looked at station characteristics.

Between 20 and 40 metres they are roughly balanced. At 40 metres and above, they lose 4.3 bikes every day, and 90% of them end the day short. 142 of the 143 stations above 50 metres lose bikes. FACTOR 4. DISTANCE TO THE NEAREST SUBWAY STATION

Farther from the subway, more bikes leave

bikes a morning at stations 661 m or more from the subway; −1.5 within 209 m

A clearer contrast in net movement than in shortage frequency.

2,714 stations in four equal quarters of distance. Net outflow: trips, 2024–2025 clear weekdays; empty share: hourly stock, 2025 dry weekdays.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Next, we looked at subway distance. Stations within about 209 metres of the subway gain bikes on average in the morning, while those 661 metres or farther away lose almost three. This is consistent with people riding toward the subway. Empty share rises from 9.6% to 12.2%, a less pronounced contrast than we saw across elevation groups. So the direction of bicycle movement and the frequency of shortages tell us different things. We then compared the station characteristics together.

FACTORS TOGETHER

Station features and running out

Station featureRank correlation with empty share (ρ)Odds ratio per 1 SD (95% CI)p
Elevation (m)0.503.53 (3.04–4.12)< 0.001
Local relief within 300 m (m)0.320.98 (0.85–1.12)0.72
Distance to nearest subway station (log)0.090.90 (0.81–1.00)0.06

Outcome: runs out, empty in at least 20% of 7–9 am readings (2025 dry weekdays): 476 of 2,695 stations. One logistic model with all three features, standardised. Elevation: odds ×2.61 for every 10 m; AUC 0.83.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Which station features go with running out? We put three of them in one logistic model. The outcome is whether a station runs out, as we defined it earlier: empty in at least one in five readings between 7 and 9 am, which holds for 476 of 2,695 stations. The first column is the rank correlation with the empty share, one feature at a time; the second is the odds ratio for one standard deviation, with all three features together. Only elevation matters. One standard deviation higher, about 13 metres, multiplies the odds of running out by 3.5; that is 2.6 times for every 10 metres. Local relief goes with running out on its own, but not once elevation is in the model, and distance to the subway hardly matters. The model tells stations that run out from those that do not with an AUC of 0.83.

FACTORS TOGETHER

Net bicycle flow runs downhill

Arrows

net flow out of each 1 km cell

69% downhill

of net flow on sloping ground, against 7% uphill (morning: 59% vs 12%)

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Each citywide arrow summarizes net bicycle movement around a 1 km cell. On sloping ground, 69% of the reported whole-day net-flow magnitude points downhill and 7% uphill. On the right, we zoom into the familiar Yonsei–Sinchon area. The red arrows show net movement toward lower ground, while blue arrows point toward higher ground. Many of the strongest connections here also run downhill. This is net movement, not the share of individual trips or evidence of how individual riders return home.

STARTING INVENTORY

Fewer bikes, more shortages

Both groups are far from the subway: the farthest distance quarter (661 m and above).

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Bikes tend to move downhill. But movement alone does not tell us whether a station runs out—the number of bicycles available at the start also matters. Here, both groups are far from the subway. Flat stations start with 19 bicycles and still have 15 at 9 am. Hill stations start with about 6, and their empty share is 28%, compared with 5% on flat ground. Despite a smaller decline in average stock, hill stations are empty more frequently. These are group averages, and stock changes can include non-trip activity. Starting inventory helps us understand shortages. A separate question is whether the bicycles lost in the morning come back later. To explore that, we classified stations using morning and full-day net outflow.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE TRUCKS

Does every hill need a truck?

?

Many stations are emptied during the 7–9 am commute.

?

Redistribution is not needed if riders return bikes on their way back home from work

→

Two criteria for station classification: Is it empty in the morning and is it empty at the end of the day?

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

What does this mean for the trucks? Should a truck rush to every station that is emptied in the morning? Not necessarily. If residents ride back home in the evening, the station refills by night and needs no truck. We call this the self-balancing hypothesis. To test it, we ask two questions of every station: is it emptied in the morning, and is it still short at the end of the day?

MORNING AND FULL-DAY NET FLOW

Four station groups

2 questions

Morning net outflow > 0? Full-day net outflow > 0?

2,843

stations, each sorted by its two answers

1,005 vs 766

G1: morning loss remains over the full day. G2: later net returns offset it.

1,771

stations have positive mean morning net outflow. Do later net returns offset it?

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

We classify stations using two signs: average net outflow during 7–9 am, and average net outflow over the full day. Positive means rentals exceed returns. G1 and G2 both lose bikes in the morning. For G1, full-day net outflow remains positive; for G2, later net returns offset the morning loss, so the full-day total is zero or negative. G3 has no net loss in either window; G4 has no morning net loss but has positive full-day net outflow. We focus on G1 and G2: 1,005 and 766 stations. These groups describe average user flow, not whether a station is empty or needs a truck.

EVENING RECOVERY

Different evening recovery

+5.3 bikes

mean net gain at a G2 station, 5–8 pm

+1.2 bikes

mean net gain at a G1 station, 5–8 pm

29 m vs 19 m

median elevation of G1 and G2; distance to the subway is similar (480 m vs 460 m)

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Both groups lose bikes in the morning, but G2 receives more net returns in the evening. From 5 to 8 pm, G2 gains an average of 5.3 bikes per station, compared with 1.2 for G1. G1 stations also have higher median elevation: 29 metres versus 19 for G2. Their median subway distances are similar, about 480 and 460 metres. This links weaker evening recovery with higher elevation, but does not establish that elevation causes the difference. The chart describes user net flow; recovery does not mean the station is full or never empty.

CONCLUSION

Insights for redistribution

Elevation is associated with persistent bicycle imbalances.

Net movement tends downhill, and G1 stations show weaker evening recovery.

Hill stations have smaller starting inventories and more frequent shortages.

Assess both which stations need redistribution and whether bikes are available before the morning commute.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Our findings point to three connected patterns. Elevation is associated with persistent bicycle imbalances. Net movement tends downhill, and stations in G1 receive fewer net returns in the evening than G2. Hill stations also start with fewer bicycles and are empty more frequently. Together, these patterns can help the city assess redistribution needs. That assessment should consider both which stations need redistribution and whether bicycles are available before the morning commute.

LIMITATIONS

Key limitations

1

Unmeasured confounding.
Other station and neighborhood factors may explain part of the associations. We cannot establish causation.

2

Unmet demand is unobserved.
We cannot count people who wanted a bicycle but found none.

3

Hourly readings miss short shortages.
Empty share describes snapshots, not continuous availability.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Three limitations matter most. First, unmeasured factors, such as land use, trip purposes or cycling infrastructure, may contribute to the associations. We cannot establish causation. Second, trip records do not capture people who wanted to rent but found no bicycle, so actual demand is not fully observed. Third, hourly stock readings can miss shortages between snapshots. Our empty share therefore describes recorded availability, not the exact proportion of time a station is empty.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

What is it about a station? We listed four candidates. Time of day, because commuting and leisure trips look different. Weather: rain and temperature. Terrain, because pedalling uphill is hard. And transit, since many people ride to and from the subway. The first two explain the days we chose; the last two are possible reasons why some stations run out. We look at them one at a time, then together.

FACTOR 2. WEATHER

Rides by daily high temperature

Each dot is one station in one band: its mean rentals on the weekdays of 2024 and 2025 whose maximum, at the nearest of 27 KMA weather stations, fell in that band (bands with 5 or more such days; 25,225 dots from 2,878 stations). Dots are spread sideways within the band so they do not overlap.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Next, weather. Rain cuts rides sharply, which is why we keep dry days; here we look at temperature. We use the day's maximum temperature where each station is, from the nearest of 27 KMA weather stations in Seoul, because a daily mean is pulled down by the night. Each dot is one station in one 5-degree band of that maximum: its mean rentals on the weekdays of 2024 and 2025 that fell in the band. The bars are the medians. On days with a high below zero the typical station sees 13 rentals. That rises to 41 at highs of 20 to 25 degrees, and then it stays flat up to 35 degrees; only above 35 there is a small dip. So it is cold that keeps people off the bikes, more than summer heat. Later we put the factors together to see how they interact.

Earlier we saw that weather changes how many people ride. Does it change where the bikes go? No. In every temperature band, from below zero to above 25 degrees, hill-top stations lose bikes, between 1.1 and 2.1 a morning, and flat stations gain them. Warm mornings move a few more bikes, cold mornings fewer, but always in the same direction.

WHEN THE TRUCKS COME

Refill timing on the hills

0.0

bikes added to a hill-top station between 1 and 6 am: nobody refills the hills overnight

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Do the trucks already fill the hills before the morning? We checked the stock at every station hour by hour. The red line is the share of hill-top stations with no bikes; the blue bars are bikes that arrive by something other than a ride, mostly trucks. Between 1 and 6 in the morning, almost nothing arrives: 0.0 bikes. So already at 6 am, 21% of the hill-top stations are empty, and by 9 it is 30%. The trucks do come, about 4.4 bikes a day, but the first big refill is from 8 to 11, once the rush has already started, and the next one is in the afternoon. The hills are refilled every day, just not in time.
